data.title: Baltimore Mayor blasts Marlon Humphrey after Raven's 'criminals' comment
data.description:
The mayor of Baltimore blasted Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey for comments the defensive back made on a podcast earlier this week disparaging the city.

Humphrey was asked during a recent episode of his podcast what Baltimore “is the best at making.”

“Criminals,” he responded before bursting out into laughter.

The comment was met with widespread condemnation online and earned him a rebuke from his team, which sent Humphrey home from the team’s trip to North Carolina to take on the Panthers this weekend.

The defensive back apologized for the comment after practice according to ESPN on Wednesday saying “as you guys know, I’ve been here my whole career. Spent lots of offseasons here. Welcomed a son here and I’m an investor in the city. And obviously, I do know the effect that words have and just like to apologize for those comments.”

Baltimore’s mayor Brandon Scott (D) was not satisfied.

“While we acknowledge Marlon’s apology, a verbal apology is not enough,” Scott said. “Baltimore is a city full of young Black boys who look to the Ravens as a beacon of light in their lives and to have someone that looks like them who wears a Baltimore Ravens jersey relegate them to becoming criminals cuts deeper.”

He added, “I wonder how he would feel if prominent Baltimoreans used their platforms to imply that Baltimore once produced great defensive backs, but we have recently lost our way.”

The mayor also noted he was inviting Humphrey “to sit down with me and some Baltimoreans who have re-entered into our community and are now preventing others from making the mistakes they made.”

Humphrey was one of several Ravens who attended a recent trip President Trump made to the Baltimore area before the midterm elections.

The Ravens won four of their first five games this season but lost to the previously winless Los Angeles Chargers on Monday.

data.title: Sanders pours cold water on 2028 White House bid
data.description:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) has poured cold water on the idea of another run for the White House. 

“I think probably not. I think taking office at 87 years of age and finishing my first term at 91 is not something that probably inspires a whole lot of people,” Sanders told host Steven Bartlett on “The Diary of a CEO” podcast. 

He later doubled down: “No, I’m not running for president.” 

The Vermont senator described his ideal candidate as someone “prepared to stand with the Working class of America” and “take on the oligarchs,” adding that he would not support a candidate “tinkering around the edges.” 

Sanders has been in Congress since 1991, spending more than a decade in the House before winning his Senate seat in 2006. He ran for president in the 2016 presidential election but lost the Democratic nod to former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton — then tried again in the 2020 cycle, dropping out to pave the way for former President Biden. 

The progressive won a fourth term in 2024 and has cited his age in contending that he won’t likely seek a fifth term in 2030. 

Asked in a 2024 interview with Politico whether this would be his last term in Congress, Sanders said: “I’m 83 now. I’ll be 89 when I get out of here. You can do the figuring. I don’t know, but I would assume, probably, yes.” 

Sanders also told Barlett this week that it’s “not a good idea” to treat elections like “beauty contests.” 

“The American people have to determine: what is their view on healthcare? Are they going to transform our healthare system? What are they going to do on AI? These questions … And then leadership will come to the fore based on how people res- feel that these candidates are responding,” he said. 

He heaped praise on Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), a progressive leader on Capitol Hill who has been increasingly seen as a potential presidential contender.

“But she’s not the only one. There are great other candidates that are out there who may not be quite as wellknown,” Sanders said. 

“You don’t know who’s going to rise up. The point that I’m making is …  I’m not a fan of what you’re doing here,” he told Barlett. “I am a fan of: here are the issues. How are the candidates going to address them? People will decide.”

data.title: Appeals court denies full panel review of McIver bid to toss case
data.description:
The Third Circuit Court of Appeals on Thursday declined a request from Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-N.J.) to have a full panel of the court weigh her bid to dismiss her pending charges after a scuffle outside an immigration detention facility.

McIver has pushed to get the case dismissed on various grounds, including that her visit to the Delaney Hall detention facility was carried out in her role as a legislative official and should be protected by prosecution under the Speech or Debate Clause. 

But in August, a three-judge panel for the court declined to toss the case, even as the panel split over a matter in which she is accused of attacking law enforcement with her forearms.

A brief notice from the court gave no rationale for the decision beyond noting the bench voted not to take up the case.

“Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power—but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver said in a statement.

“Now, due to the disappointing decision by the Third Circuit, we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”

McIver could appeal the ruling to the Supreme Court, and the lawmaker said in her statement that she and her legal team “are looking at every possible option for what comes next.”

Over the summer the three-judge panel declined to toss the case on a number of grounds raised by McIver, finding that while her inspection of Delaney Hall was protected under the clause, her intervention in the arrest of Newark Mayor Ras Baraka (D) was not.

But one judge dissented, saying McIver’s “plausibly incidental contact” with one of the officers came as she was being impeded from carrying out her legislative duties by touring the controversial detention center.

He also touched on McIver’s claims that the case amounted to a selective prosecution, saying the lawmaker “presented enough [evidence] to obtain discovery on whether this prosecution ‘was intended to prevent [her] exercise of a fundamental right’” to conduct legislative oversight.

McIver is now slated to face trial in the case, though an earlier trial date set for this month has not been rescheduled while motions were pending.

data.title: Trump says he doesn't need help from Russia, China to end Iran war
data.description:
President Trump on Wednesday said he does not need Russia and China’s help to conclude the Iran war, before meeting with the leaders of both countries for an unprecedented summit in China the following day.

“Well, you know, we don’t need any help,” Trump told Fox News’s Jacqui Heinrich while in Shenzhen, China. “We’ve defeated [Iran’s] navy, we’ve defeated their air force, we’ve defeated their anti-aircraft. Their missiles are down to about 12 –– they still have some missiles, but they’re down to about 12, 13 percent of what they were.”

“And they want to make a deal,” he added. “So, I don’t need help. I mean, I’m not going to go and ask them for help.”

Trump said Iran has treated the U.S. “very well” and that they “haven’t fired, they haven’t put ships in the water.”

The president did not acknowledge Iranian strikes on a U.S. air base in Kuwait on Wednesday or multiple one-way drone attacks on a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain on Tuesday, following similar strikes, including a U.S. strike on Qeshm Island, late last week.

Iran has ramped up its attacks on U.S. targets and allies in the region after both sides have largely held off on retaliatory strikes since September. Washington and Tehran have sought a diplomatic end to the war, which began on Feb. 28. 

Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a historic 90-minute trilateral meeting. All three leaders released a four-point “peace declaration” calling for promoting reforms at the United Nations “so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges.”

The declaration added “that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction” and reaffirmed that a nuclear war must never be fought. The leaders also said they intend to “increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.”

Trump told reporters before the summit that he wanted to discuss the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war with Xi and Putin.

China and Russia have both supported Iran by buying its oil, reportedly providing intelligence and maintaining trade ties, to help Tehran resist U.S. military and economic pressure. Both countries have denied aiding Iran in its fight against the U.S.

Trump received a boost of support from some Republican lawmakers back home, but others hope the president knows that, as Rep. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) said, “China and Russia are not our friends though.”

Alabama Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville (R), soon to no longer be one of the state’s senators, previously told The Hill that he did not care who Trump is meeting with, “we’ve got to get this over with,” referring to the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

“They’re all involved in some form or fashion,” Tuberville said. “So you bring all the leaders of the world together and try to work it out. I mean, I’d rather him do that than sit over here and worry about air traffic control.”

data.title: Live updates: Trump, Xi, Putin issue peace declaration; Democrats' Iran war powers resolution fails again
data.description:
GOP senators again blocked a Democrat-backed resolution directing President Trump to withdraw U.S. troops from the conflict with Iran, despite the war contributing to Republicans’ sweeping losses in November’s midterms.

Three Republicans voted with nearly the entire Senate Democratic caucus for the war powers resolution, which failed on a 48-51 vote after passing in the House over the summer. Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) was again the only Democrat to vote against it, and Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy (Conn.) was not present — as he is recovering from a stroke.

Meanwhile, President Trump is heading back to Washington Thursday after a rare trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. The trio issued a declaration toward peace during the discussions.

“It was a Great and Highly Consequential Trip,” Trump wrote in a Thursday afternoon Truth Social post, in which he also announced plans to hold a Friday news conference about the visit.

Ahead of the talks, some viewed the meeting as a poor signal of where U.S. priorities lie, while others commended the president for his willingness to have hard conversations with less friendly countries.

Lawmakers are also staring down a Dec. 11 government funding deadline, with neither party settled on a strategy to avoid a shutdown. Republicans have made little progress on full-year spending bills, making another short-term funding extension increasingly likely.

Follow live below.

data.title: Hillary Clinton: Xi, Putin play Trump 'like a child's guitar'
data.description:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin play President Trump “like a child’s guitar.”

“All [Trump] cares about, the best I can tell, is looking like he belongs in the company of Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, both of whom he’s going to meet with, together,” Clinton said in a Wednesday episode of the “High Stakes” podcast with journalist Kara Swisher.

“I mean, these two men play him like a child’s guitar,” she added. “It is pathetic.”

Trump, Xi and Putin issued a four-point “peace declaration” in the wake of a trilateral summit in China on Thursday. Trump has had notably warm relationships with the leaders of the two U.S. adversaries. 

The three leaders discussed United Nations reform, oil production and supply, the International Criminal Court and nuclear conflict, according to all three countries.

The peace declaration says that with their status as permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, the countries are “committed to promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges” and intend to plan to “increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.”

Trump greeted Putin as a “friend” on Thursday as the two arrived for a meeting. 

“Who is he? He’s my friend.” Trump is heard saying after walking into a room with his Russian counterpart.

Earlier this week, the president told reporters he believed the Russian president was “backing down a bit” in the war in Ukraine, which will hit the five-year mark next February.

“I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump said. “I think he’s backing down. I think he’d like to, frankly, I think he’d like to see it finished.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

data.title: Watch live: Van Hollen, Merkley push Senate reforms amid Democratic leadership fight
data.description:
Sens. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) will deliver remarks on Thursday calling for changes to Senate rules and Democratic Caucus procedures next year, following the party’s midterm victories.

The lawmakers are pushing to remove procedural roadblocks that have stalled legislation while giving rank-and-file Democrats, including newly elected senators, a greater voice in shaping the party’s agenda.

The push comes amid a heated Democratic leadership battle in the Senate, with Van Hollen challenging Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) over the party’s direction as Democrats prepare to take control of the chamber in January.

The event is scheduled to begin at 3 p.m. EST.

Watch live above.

data.title: Senate Republicans reject war powers resolution to end Iran war
data.description:
Senate Republicans on Wednesday blocked a measure that would have directed President Trump to end hostilities in Iran.

It’s not the first time such a measure has come up for a vote in the Senate this year, but Democrats hoped for success after a midterm election that saw many voters support Democrats out of opposition to the conflict.

The vote failed 48-51. GOP Sens. Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and Rand Paul (Ky.),who have voted for previous resolutions directing Trump to end the war, joined almost the entire Democratic caucus.

Centrist Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), an ardent supporter of Israel, was the only Democrat to vote against it. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who voted for the resolution in September, voted against the current version.

“I’ve supported some. I mean, you do know resolutions differ from each one. This one doesn’t go to the president, so it’s just a statement from Congress,” Tillis told reporters. “I’ve made that statement. I don’t need to vote on a Democrat resolution to make that statement.”

The measure, known as a war powers resolution, is mostly a signaling vote. Democrats wanted to put Republicans on the record voting against ending the war, even though if the resolution had passed, Trump would likely not have signed it. 

Thursday’s vote was the first time either chamber voted on the war powers resolution since the November midterms. 

The House passed a complementary resolution in mid-September, led by Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.), by a vote of 220-204. Seven Republicans joined Democrats in that case to limit Trump’s military actions against Iran. 

The Senate war powers vote comes as the cost of the conflict has gone up since October, when it was just over $47 billion.

Arthur Miller, the deputy comptroller for Budget and Appropriations Affairs at the Pentagon, told Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) during a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on Thursday that the updated cost of the Iran war is $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13. 

The figure includes munitions costs, equipment replacement costs and operational costs, but does not include the totality of damage to U.S. military facilities in the Middle East.

data.title: DOJ, DHS launch hub to fight cybercrime
data.description:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Justice Department (DOJ) announced a new hub to combat online cybercrime Wednesday, specifically targeting criminal scams and sextortion schemes. 

The launch comes amid growing concern after a series of tech outages in recent days, though the government has insisted there is no indication cyberattacks were responsible.

More than 30 federal agencies along with hundreds of state and local partners are part of the initiative, which will connect public and private entities to help stop cybercriminals.

“It gives investigators tools to triage victim complaints and map the networks responsible. It also provides a direct channel to the private-sector organizations best positioned to facilitate outreach to victims and disrupt criminal operations, as well as dedicated technical support,” the DOJ said in a statement.

The government will also use AI-powered tools through a private partner, TRM Labs, the DOJ said.

President Trump previously ordered multiple federal departments and agencies to create the center to combat cyber crime in a March executive order.

“Cybercrime, fraud, and predatory schemes are draining American families of their life savings, stealing the benefits of years of work, and destroying the lives of our youth,” he wrote in the order.

Cybercrime and sextortion schemes have become a growing concern, especially amid the rise of AI. The FBI said last week that North Korean hackers had stolen more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 months. And some recent hacks have even occurred without human involvement; top AI companies publicly identified instances of their unreleased models escaping and hacking other companies.

The AI boom and accompanying cybercrime has already been a focus for lawmakers in Washington. Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), with the support of First Lady Melania Trump, co-sponsored the Take It Down Act, a law that criminalized the publication of sexually explicit deepfake images online. The law, signed in 2025, recorded its first conviction in April.

Trump administration officials participated the annual worldwide threats hearing on Capitol Hill Wednesday, where the recent outages involving U.S. air traffic, financial institutions and even the NSA were top of mind for lawmakers.

data.title: O'Reilly suggests building technology like Iron Dome to prevent hackers: 'They're not going away'
data.description:
Conservative commentator Bill O’Reilly said there should be a bipartisan effort to develop technology like the “Iron Dome” to protect the U.S.’s technology infrastructure against hackers.

“Both parties are going to have to say, look, we have to develop technology just as we did with the Iron Dome and the space weaponry, all that, to protect our infrastructure from hackers, because they’re not going away,” O’Reilly said during an appearance on NewsNation’s “Katie Pavlich Tonight.”

O’Reilly’s suggestion comes as Americans are recovering from widespread technology outages in the past week that have impacted flights, banking systems and more.

On Nov. 12, Microsoft faced global outages that impacted its platforms Outlook and Teams. The incident, which lasted about a day, was “introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company said.

A day later, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours. Authorities attributed the incident to an overload of data on routers. Thousands of flights were delayed and canceled on Friday, impacting operations through the weekend.

Customers of several banks including Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo had trouble accessing their accounts on Monday. A spokesperson from JPMorgan Chase told The Hill the cause was “a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems” and denied anything “cyber-related.”

Speculations flared over whether the outages are linked to a cyberattack, but, Trump administration officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, have repeatedly said that is not the case.

In a Fox News interview, Mullin noted that he could say with “98 percent certainty” that the outages were not linked to cyberattack but said “SI” or super intelligence could have been the reason.

Chase said on the social platform X on Thursday that “third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack.”

“Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,” the company added.

Raising concerns over hackers during the NewsNation interview, O’Reilly said, “There are millions of them. And they’re mercenaries. They’re criminals. They’re awful. And they can destroy lives. They can destroy countries.”

On Tuesday, the National Security Agency (NSA) faced a network outage which disrupted the operations of NSANet, a classified internal network used by employees.

“They got into the NSA stuff today,” O’Reilly said. “The hackers got in. Now, don’t tell me that’s a functional thing. It’s not. These are targeted things.”

O’Reilly emphasized that when President Trump returns from his trip to China where he took part in a rare three-way talk with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, “he has to bring in all his tech people and security people and figure this out.”
